idiom_name: TaskCompletionSource in a ConcurrentDictionary + Task.WaitAsync deadline
implementation_notes: async/await plus TaskCompletionSource replaces the callback registry: the caller parks a TaskCompletionSource in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by the request's correlation id and awaits it, while the reply pump looks the id up and calls SetResult/SetException. Task.WaitAsync supplies the deadline and the caller's CancellationToken supplies cancellation; System.Threading.Channels gives the same shape in-process, where the reply channel can simply be a ChannelWriter handed to the requester. The classic reply queue survives as the dictionary plus the reply subscription.
pitfalls: Create the TaskCompletionSource with RunContinuationsAsynchronously; otherwise the reply-pump thread runs the caller's continuation inline and a slow continuation stalls every other reply.
Complete the source on the reply pump and never block there: a consumer thread calling .Result or .Wait() deadlocks under a SynchronizationContext.
An entry not removed in a finally block leaks, and a duplicate or late reply then completes a TaskCompletionSource nobody observes.

variants.name: MassTransit IRequestClient request/response
variants.implementation_notes: MassTransit owns the whole pattern: GetResponse<TResponse>(request, cancellationToken, timeout) returns a Task, the bus carries the response address and request id, a consumer failure comes back as a Fault<T> and surfaces as a RequestFaultException, and the request timeout (default 30 seconds) also sets the message time-to-live. Use it when the service bus is already in the stack; the trade is a framework and DI-based configuration for what is otherwise a few lines of correlation-table code.
pitfalls: A cancelled GetResponse stops the wait but leaves the request in the queue until it is consumed or its TTL expires, so the consumer must be idempotent.
Faults arrive as a Fault<T> message and surface as RequestFaultException; catching only timeouts hides the domain-error path.
